cleanRule: EES = causal explanation + evidence from stimulus where provided
leaderboardTip: ~60% of HSC questions are Explain/Analyse type — causal connectives (SO, BECAUSE, BUT) are essential.

dotPoints.label: 5-1a
dotPoints.text: Investigate evidence for the origin of organic molecules on the Earth, including Urey and Miller's experiments, communities around black smokers, and meteorites/panspermia

dotPoints.label: 5-1b
dotPoints.text: Investigate the evidence for the development of photosynthetic life, including cyanobacteria and stromatolites

dotPoints.label: 5-1c
dotPoints.text: Evaluate the evidence for the origin of multicellular life and resulting changes to ecosystems, for example the Ediacaran and Cambrian fauna

dotPoints.label: 5-1d
dotPoints.text: Investigate the conquest of land by both plants and animals

topics.title: Changes in the Geosphere, Atmosphere and Hydrosphere

dotPoints.label: 5-2a
dotPoints.text: Analyse the changes in the geosphere, atmosphere and hydrosphere that resulted from the development and evolution of the biosphere, including the effect of photosynthesising cyanobacteria on each of the spheres, and the role of oxygen in the production of banded iron formations

dotPoints.label: 5-3a
dotPoints.text: Model the plate tectonic supercycle

dotPoints.label: 5-3b
dotPoints.text: Outline the effect of the plate tectonic supercycle on large-scale phenomena, including climate and evolution

dotPoints.label: 5-4a
dotPoints.text: Investigate and model processes of fossil formation by examining a variety of methods in rock, including mould formations, cast formations, and trace fossils

dotPoints.label: 5-4b
dotPoints.text: Discuss the significance of index fossils in generating a geological timescale

dotPoints.label: 5-4c
dotPoints.text: Extrapolate how the principles of uniformitarianism and superposition as well as fossils and absolute dating can be used to date events of geological significance, for example the evolution of the Cambrian fauna and mass extinction events

dotPoints.label: 6-1a
dotPoints.text: Using data, predict the zones along which earthquakes and both effusive and explosive volcanic eruptions are likely to occur and relate these to plate boundaries

dotPoints.label: 6-1b
dotPoints.text: Using secondary sources, investigate and model the changing depth of the focus of earthquakes at convergent and divergent boundaries

dotPoints.label: 6-1c
dotPoints.text: Using secondary sources, investigate and explain the hazards associated with earthquakes, including ground motion and tsunamis

dotPoints.label: 6-1d
dotPoints.text: Using secondary sources, investigate and explain the hazards associated with volcanoes, for example ash eruptions and lava flows, lahars and poisonous gas emissions

dotPoints.label: 6-1e
dotPoints.text: Account for the types of magma in each of the above types of volcanoes, and analyse how this affects the explosivity of their eruptions

dotPoints.label: 6-1f
dotPoints.text: Investigate the point at which a geological hazard becomes a disaster

topics.title: Impact of Natural Disasters on the Biosphere

dotPoints.label: 6-2a
dotPoints.text: Using data from secondary sources, compare the eruptions that occur at explosive and effusive volcanoes in terms of the impact on the biosphere and atmosphere

dotPoints.label: 6-2b
dotPoints.text: Analyse the effects of a major volcanic eruption on the atmosphere in terms of changing the climate, both warming and cooling

dotPoints.label: 6-2c
dotPoints.text: In a case study, investigate one eruption that has had a significant effect on the biosphere and atmosphere and assess its impact, including but not limited to Mount Pinatubo

dotPoints.label: 6-2d
dotPoints.text: Evaluate the causes and physical impact of climatic phenomena on a local ecosystem, including hailstorms, east coast lows, droughts or floods, and bushfires

dotPoints.label: 6-2e
dotPoints.text: Investigate how human activities can contribute to the frequency and magnitude of some natural disasters, including droughts or floods, and bushfires and landslides

topics.title: Prediction and Prevention of Natural Disasters

dotPoints.label: 6-3a
dotPoints.text: Using secondary sources, evaluate the effectiveness of technologies in predicting natural disasters, for example volcanoes: three-dimensional imaging, seismic data, early-warning systems, ground-movement data, analysis of historical data; earthquakes: ground movement detectors, anomalous animal behaviour, strain meters; east coast lows: temperatures, pressure systems

dotPoints.label: 6-3b
dotPoints.text: Investigate and evaluate the technologies used to minimise the effect of natural disasters associated with volcanoes and earthquakes, including building codes, disaster warning systems and education

dotPoints.label: 6-3c
dotPoints.text: Using secondary sources, assess the accuracy of technologies used in meteorology to predict and prevent damage to life and infrastructure as a result of natural weather events

topics.title: Natural Processes of Variations in Climate

dotPoints.label: 7-1a
dotPoints.text: Use modelling to explain the causes of the natural greenhouse effect and examine the timescales in which changes occur

dotPoints.label: 7-1b
dotPoints.text: Using secondary sources, assess the different causes of natural climate variation and the timescales in which changes occur, including the plate tectonic supercycle, massive volcanic eruptions in the Deccan and Siberian Traps, changes in the Earth's orbit around the Sun, and changes in ocean currents and ocean circulation

dotPoints.label: 7-2a
dotPoints.text: Describe and discuss ancient evidence of variations in global temperature, including pollen grains in sedimentary rocks, changes in rock types, fossils and microfossils, and changing isotope ratios in rocks and deep sea sediments

dotPoints.label: 7-2b
dotPoints.text: Identify and explain more recent evidence of climate variation, including ice cores containing gas bubbles and oxygen isotopes, dendrochronology, Aboriginal art sites showing now-extinct species and environments, human instrumental records, and isotope ratios shown in stalagmites, stalactites and corals

topics.title: Influence of Human Activities on Changes to Climate

dotPoints.label: 7-3a
dotPoints.text: Distinguish between the natural greenhouse effect and any anthropogenic greenhouse effects

dotPoints.label: 7-3b
dotPoints.text: Investigate any influence that human activities may have had on the environment since the Industrial Revolution, including increases in greenhouse gases and ocean acidification

dotPoints.label: 7-3c
dotPoints.text: Investigate flow-on effects of changes to climate, including changing weather patterns, changes in glaciers, sea ice and ice sheets, and changing range of species due to rising sea level

topics.title: Mitigation and Adaptation Strategies

dotPoints.label: 7-4a
dotPoints.text: Investigate possible human-induced causes for the enhanced greenhouse effect, including the burning of fossil fuels for energy and land use and land cover change

dotPoints.label: 7-4b
dotPoints.text: Investigate scientific evidence suggesting ways in which humans may assist to minimise any human contribution to the greenhouse effect in their daily lives

dotPoints.label: 7-4c
dotPoints.text: Evaluate scientific evidence for the usefulness of a range of mitigation and adaptation strategies, including urban design and geo-engineering strategies, alternative energy sources, and using or changing agricultural practices including those of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples

keywords: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples

dotPoints.label: 8-1a
dotPoints.text: Identify Australian renewable resources and where they are located, including agricultural resources (terrestrial and aquatic), water, and energy sources

dotPoints.label: 8-1b
dotPoints.text: Investigate how mining sites affect the environment, including Aboriginal cultural sites, and examine methods of reclamation of the environment after mining operations cease, including open-pit mining, underground mining methods, and offshore and onshore drilling

dotPoints.label: 8-1c
dotPoints.text: Prepare a case study to investigate the involvement of traditional owners in the planning procedures, mining practices and restoration of damaged lands after mining operations cease

dotPoints.label: 8-1d
dotPoints.text: Prepare a case study of an important Australian renewable or non-renewable resource, including how the resource is found, extracted and/or managed, how the resource is used, whether the resource can be extracted and/or used sustainably, and the past, present and future use and importance of the resource

dotPoints.label: 8-2a
dotPoints.text: Conduct a practical investigation of the composition of household or organisational waste

dotPoints.label: 8-2b
dotPoints.text: Outline the management options for different types of solid waste

dotPoints.label: 8-2c
dotPoints.text: Evaluate the sustainability of a named waste management option, for example energy used to produce and/or recycle the waste, environmental impact of waste disposal, space for disposal or storage of waste, local waste management facilities, and demand for reused or recycled waste

topics.title: Sustainability

dotPoints.label: 8-3a
dotPoints.text: Investigate different definitions of sustainability and the rationales that underpin those definitions

dotPoints.label: 8-3b
dotPoints.text: Investigate human activities that affect sustainability, including overharvesting, water pollution, and habitat removal or destruction

dotPoints.label: 8-3c
dotPoints.text: Investigate the processes used by Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples as sustainable resource managers, for example cultural traditions that preserve Country and Place, ongoing engagement with land councils, national parks and municipal councils, and legislation and actions to protect significant areas of Country and Place

dotPoints.label: 8-3d
dotPoints.text: Research and present information about a sustainability initiative in their community

keywords: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples

bandRules.course: NSW HSC Earth and Environmental Science
bandRules.purpose: Rules for generating model responses aligned to HSC performance band expectations.

always: Align all content to the NSW HSC Earth and Environmental Science syllabus.
Answer the directive verb exactly as asked.
Keep all claims relevant to the question and stimulus.
Do not include content beyond syllabus requirements for full marks unless it directly improves clarity without changing the expected standard.
Use examples only when they strengthen the answer.
Avoid vague phrases such as 'things', 'stuff', 'it affects the Earth a lot'.

identify: Name the required feature, process, example, or component.
Do not explain unless the question demands it.
outline: Provide the main features or general idea.
describe: State relevant characteristics and what they do or show.
Include features and function where appropriate.
explain: Link ideas using explicit scientific reasoning.
analyse: Show relationships, patterns, or causes and effects.
Use evidence, data, or examples where available.
assess: Make a judgement based on strengths and limitations.
evaluate: Judge overall value, usefulness, effectiveness, or significance.
Include strengths, limitations, and a clear final judgement.
justify: Give reasons that support a conclusion or choice.
account: Give reasons for why something occurs.
predict: State the most likely future outcome based on scientific evidence, trends, or principles.

stimulus_rules: If a graph, table, map, diagram, or data is provided, directly refer to it.
Use exact trends, patterns, or features from the stimulus where possible.
Do not ignore the stimulus in higher-mark questions.

Band6.nesa_descriptor: Demonstrates extensive knowledge and understanding of scientific concepts, including complex and abstract ideas. Communicates scientific understanding succinctly and consistently using correct and precise scientific terms in a variety of formats and contexts. Designs investigations to obtain accurate, reliable and valid data, evaluating and mitigating risks and making modifications in response to evidence. Selects, processes, interprets and represents qualitative and quantitative data to derive trends, show patterns and relationships, explain phenomena and make predictions. Designs solutions to scientific problems or hypotheses using primary and secondary data and scientific evidence. Applies knowledge and information to unfamiliar situations to propose comprehensive solutions or explanations for scientific issues or scenarios.
Band6.knowledge_standard: Extensive knowledge and understanding of scientific concepts, including complex and abstract ideas.
must_include: Accurate and precise scientific terminology used consistently.
Logical and coherent sequencing of ideas.
Explicit causal links where relevant.
Relevant examples, evidence, or data integrated into the response.
Clear interpretation of trends, patterns, relationships, or processes from data or stimulus.
Explanation of phenomena and prediction of outcomes where required.
Application to unfamiliar situations with comprehensive solutions or explanations.
A direct, well-supported judgement for assess/evaluate/justify questions.
For investigations: consideration of accuracy, reliability, validity, risk mitigation, and evidence-based modifications.
style_rules: Communicate succinctly and consistently — avoid padding.
Integrate multiple ideas rather than listing disconnected facts.
Link mechanisms to outcomes and consequences.
Where relevant, move from process to consequence to significance.
Represent data and understanding across a variety of formats and contexts where required.
avoid: Word count inflation without additional scientific depth.

short_response_2_3_marks: Directly answer the question in the first sentence.
Include at least one explicit scientific link or mechanism.
mid_response_4_6_marks: Use evidence, examples, or data if available.
extended_response_7_plus_marks: Address all parts of the question.

Band5.nesa_descriptor: Demonstrates thorough knowledge and understanding of scientific concepts, including complex and abstract ideas. Communicates scientific understanding logically and effectively using correct scientific terms in a variety of formats and contexts. Designs investigations to obtain reliable and valid data, evaluating and mitigating risks and making some modifications in response to evidence. Selects, processes, interprets and represents qualitative and quantitative data to derive trends, show patterns and relationships. Designs solutions to scientific problems or hypotheses using primary and secondary data and scientific evidence. Applies knowledge and information to unfamiliar situations to propose explanations for scientific issues or scenarios.
Band5.knowledge_standard: Thorough knowledge and understanding of scientific concepts, including complex and abstract ideas, but less extensive or precise than Band 6.
must_include: Correct scientific terminology used logically and effectively.
Clear explanation of key concepts with mostly sound reasoning.
Interpretation of data to derive trends, patterns, or relationships.
Application to unfamiliar situations to propose explanations (but less comprehensive than Band 6).
Relevant example or evidence where useful.
For investigations: consideration of reliability, validity, and risk, with some modifications in response to evidence.
style_rules: Communicate logically and effectively across a variety of formats.
May be less integrated, less precise, or less succinctly expressed than Band 6.
avoid: Ignoring the stimulus or data where provided.

Band4.nesa_descriptor: Demonstrates sound knowledge and understanding of scientific concepts. Communicates scientific understanding effectively using scientific terms. Designs and plans investigations to obtain data, and evaluates risks. Processes, interprets and represents data using a range of scientific formats. Identifies scientific problems, questions or hypotheses and applies processes to primary or secondary data. Applies knowledge and information relevant to scientific issues or scenarios.
Band4.knowledge_standard: Sound knowledge and understanding of scientific concepts, without the depth or complexity of Band 5 or 6.
must_include: Correct scientific terminology used effectively.
Clear explanation of core concepts.
Processing and interpretation of data using scientific formats.
Identification of scientific problems or hypotheses with application to data.
Application of knowledge to relevant scientific issues or scenarios.
For investigations: design and planning to obtain data, with risk evaluation.
style_rules: May be less detailed, less precise, or less well linked than Band 5 or 6.
Interpretation present but may lack depth or connection to broader concepts.

Band3.nesa_descriptor: Demonstrates basic knowledge and understanding of scientific concepts. Communicates scientific understanding using basic scientific terms. Implements scientific processes to obtain data, and identifies risks. Processes primary or secondary data, and represents it using scientific formats. Responds to scientific problems, questions, or hypotheses. Recalls scientific knowledge and information.
Band3.knowledge_standard: Basic knowledge and understanding of scientific concepts, with limited depth or connection between ideas.
must_include: Some correct scientific facts or knowledge.
Basic scientific terms used, though not always precisely.
Simple response to a scientific problem, question, or hypothesis.
Basic processing or representation of primary or secondary data.
Recall of relevant scientific knowledge or information.
For investigations: implementation of processes and identification of risks.
style_rules: Communication is simple and may lack precision.
avoid: Invented or incorrect science presented as fact.

Band2.nesa_descriptor: Demonstrates limited knowledge and understanding of scientific concepts. Communicates scientific understanding using limited scientific terms. Partially outlines investigations to obtain data and information. Provides simple descriptions of scientific phenomena. Recalls basic scientific knowledge and information.
Band2.knowledge_standard: Limited knowledge and understanding; responses are partial, underdeveloped, and mostly descriptive.
must_include: A few isolated correct ideas or basic facts.
Very limited use of scientific language.
Simple descriptions of scientific phenomena.
Recall of basic scientific knowledge or information.
For investigations: partial outline only.
style_rules: Communication is minimal and uses limited scientific terms.
avoid: Presenting Band 2 as a complete or adequate response.

Band1.nesa_descriptor: Performance reported as Band 1 indicates that the minimum standard expected was not demonstrated.
Band1.knowledge_standard: Does not demonstrate the minimum expected standard.
must_include: No generation target. Used only as a fallback classification label for wholly inadequate responses.
Formula or method used.
Substitution of values.
Working shown clearly.
Final answer with correct unit.
Reasonable significant figures where appropriate.
Independent variable.
Dependent variable.
Controlled variables.
Method steps in logical order.
Reference to reliability, accuracy, validity, and risk where relevant.
Quote or paraphrase the main trend, pattern, or anomaly.
Use comparative language such as increase, decrease, peak, lower, higher, fluctuates.
Link the pattern to scientific concepts.
Do not merely restate the graph without interpretation.
Opening sentence that addresses the question directly.
Body paragraphs organised by concept or argument.
Concluding sentence with judgement if required.

Band6_explain: State the key scientific process or concept.
Explain the mechanism using precise terminology.
State the resulting consequence, significance, or broader Earth system impact.
Band6_analyse: Identify the major components or factors.
Show how they interact or relate.
Interpret any trend, pattern, relationship, or evidence.
Link these relationships back to the question.
Band6_evaluate: State the issue, strategy, technology, or process being evaluated.
Explain at least one strength with evidence.
Explain at least one limitation with evidence.
Make a clear final judgement using phrases such as 'overall', 'therefore', or 'this is effective to a large extent'.
Band6_assess: State the issue and the criteria for judgement.
Discuss positive aspects and negative aspects.
Conclude with a balanced but definite judgement.
Band6_justify: State the chosen option or conclusion clearly.
Link each reason back to the question.
Finish with a sentence that confirms why the judgement is valid.

before_output: Has the directive verb been answered correctly?
Has every part of the question been addressed?
Is the terminology appropriate to the target band?
Are the causal links or relationships clear?
Has the stimulus been used where relevant?
Has a judgement been made when required?
band6_checklist: Response is coherent and logically sequenced.
Judgement is explicit if required by the question.

target_band_selection_rule.Band6: Generate with extensive precision, integrated reasoning across complex and abstract ideas, evidence, prediction, and strong judgement. Responses must be succinct and consistently use precise scientific terminology.
target_band_selection_rule.Band5: Generate with thorough, logically sound explanation and clear terminology. Slightly less integrated or precise than Band 6; applies to unfamiliar situations but with less comprehensiveness.
target_band_selection_rule.Band4: Generate with sound core content, effective use of scientific terms, and clear structure. Interpret data and apply knowledge to relevant scenarios, but with reduced depth and sophistication.
target_band_selection_rule.Band3: Generate basic, mostly descriptive responses using simple scientific terms. Recall facts and respond simply to problems. Limited explanation and basic data processing only.
target_band_selection_rule.Band2: Generate very simple, partial, and underdeveloped responses using minimal scientific language. Simple descriptions and basic recall only.
target_band_selection_rule.Band1: Do not intentionally generate unless explicitly requested as a wholly inadequate response example.

forbidden_behaviours: Do not generate Band 6 responses by merely increasing word count.
Do not add irrelevant advanced content to imitate sophistication.
Do not ignore the syllabus or stimulus.
Do not use vague judgements such as 'it is good' without criteria.
